system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-05-12 13:34:00 to 2186-05-14 10:23:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and orthostatic hypotension was admitted for evaluation of intermittent chest pressure over two days, associated with nausea and diaphoresis. Initial concerns for acute coronary syndrome were raised due to his cardiac history, but serial troponins were negative and EKG showed only transient ST depressions. A chest x-ray revealed no acute process, and an exercise stress echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular function with no evidence of inducible ischemia. His symptoms were attributed to dehydration, exacerbated by his mitochondrial disease, which also caused a transient rise in creatinine from baseline. He was treated with 2 liters of IV normal saline, restarted on clopidogrel after a 5-day hold, and continued on his baseline cardiac medications. His condition improved, and he was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to maintain hydration and follow up with his primary care physician and cardiologist.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You’re here because of chest pain and dizziness after your IVIG infusion yesterday. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, during the IVIG, I had a burning chest pain for about five minutes. It went away, but then at home, I had pressure in my chest at night, not with activity, and I felt lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your cardiologist checked your blood pressure and found a big drop when you stood up—about 40 points. That’s called orthostatic hypotension. Has this happened before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it happens a lot after IVIG. I think it’s related to my mitochondrial disease. I get weak and dizzy when I’m dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve reviewed your records. You’ve had similar episodes before. We’re not worried about a heart attack this time because your EKG is stable and your troponin levels came back normal twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why does this keep happening after IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not entirely sure. One theory is that IVIG might trigger a mild immune reaction—something called capillary leak—where fluid shifts out of your blood vessels, making you low on volume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so weak and dizzy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And when your blood pressure drops, it can cause chest pressure, especially with your history. But your heart tests are reassuring—no signs of blockage or strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a stress test recently, and it was fine. So this isn’t my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the cardiology team agrees—this is non-cardiac chest pain. Likely due to the combination of orthostatic drop and your underlying mitochondrial condition affecting how your body handles stress and volume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So what are we doing now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV fluids at 250 cc per hour to rehydrate you. That should help stabilize your blood pressure and ease the chest discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Should I stop anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping all your usual medications—like aspirin, Plavix, your blood pressure and cholesterol pills. But we’re watching your blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take Valsartan in the morning. Should I skip it on IVIG days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, that’s a good point. We’re recommending that on days you get IVIG, you hold your morning Valsartan to avoid too much blood pressure drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll tell my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also sent a special blood test called CH50 to check if your immune system reacted to the IVIG. It’s a send-out test, so results will take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will that tell us?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the CH50 is low, it might suggest complement activation—part of that capillary leak theory. But even if it is, we don’t think it’s severe. You don’t have swelling or other signs of a serious reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s more about understanding the pattern than treating something new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want your doctors to have all the info to manage your IVIG infusions more safely in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I just reviewed your repeat vital signs. Your blood pressure is stable now, and when we checked you sitting and standing, there’s no big drop anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel better. The chest pressure is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That supports our idea that this was related to low volume and orthostasis. We’ll keep you on fluids overnight and monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m checking in on you. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’ve had no chest pain overnight, and I walked to the bathroom without dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs from this morning are normal—kidney function, blood count, everything. Your troponin was checked again and is still negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow morning. We want to make sure you stay stable through the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the compression stockings? You mentioned TEDs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, wearing compression stockings can help reduce blood pooling in your legs and prevent orthostatic drops. We recommend wearing them during the day, especially on IVIG days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll get a pair. My doctor has been trying to set up home IV fluids, but it’s been delayed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would help a lot. Staying well-hydrated before and after IVIG could prevent these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. No changes to your medications. You’ll continue everything as before, just with those two adjustments on IVIG days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hold morning Valsartan and wear compression stockings. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. And your primary care doctor will follow up on the CH50 test result when it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably not, but it helps confirm whether IVIG is triggering a mild immune response. Either way, the management is the same—hydration and blood pressure precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home. Your condition is stable, and you’ve had no symptoms since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to recap: no heart attack, your chest pain was non-cardiac, likely from orthostatic hypotension after IVIG. We hydrated you, and you improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should keep doing the same things at home, just adjust for IVIG days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay hydrated, wear your compression stockings, hold your morning Valsartan on infusion days, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my records reflect that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve sent all the details to your primary care provider. You’re cleared to go home with your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I know my case is complicated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, hypogammaglobulinemia, and orthostatic hypotension was admitted for evaluation of chest pain and lightheadedness following an IVIG infusion. His symptoms were consistent with prior episodes, occurring in the setting of orthostatic hypotension without evidence of cardiac ischemia, as confirmed by normal serial troponins, unchanged EKG, and recent negative stress test. He was treated with IV hydration, which resolved his orthostatic symptoms. Management focused on preventive strategies, including holding the morning dose of Valsartan on IVIG infusion days and wearing compression stockings. A CH50 level was sent to evaluate for complement activation, with results to be followed up outpatient. He was discharged home in stable condition with no changes to his baseline medications.
